source.title: The Top Unsolved Questions in Mathematics Remain Mostly Mysterious

accepted.question_text: Is a three-dimensional sphere determined, in the topological sense described in the source, by simple connectivity? In other words, if a three-dimensional surface has the property that any loop drawn on it can be continuously shrunk to a single point without tearing the loop or lifting it off the surface, does that property characterize the sphere among such three-dimensional surfaces?

evidence.quote: According to CMI, the Poincaré conjecture focuses on a topological question about whether spheres with three-dimensional surfaces are ‘essentially characterized’ by a property called ‘simple connectivity.’ That property means that if you encase the surface of the sphere with a rubber band, you can compress that band—without tearing it or removing it from the surface—until it is just a single point.
In 2010 CMI announced that Perelman had proved the conjecture and, along the way, had also solved the late mathematician William Thurston’s related geometrization conjecture.

accepted.question_text: Is every problem whose solution can be verified easily also a problem whose solution can be found easily? Using the terminology stated in the source, is the class P of questions with solutions that are easy to find the same as the class NP of questions with solutions that are easy to verify?

evidence.quote: This problem concerns the issue of whether questions with solutions that are easy to find (a class of queries called P) are also easy to verify (a class called NP).

evidence.quote: When people have tried to pin me down to a number, Aaronson says, I’ll give a 97 percent or 98 percent chance that P is not equal to NP.
